newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan c/a surplus could pose problems--US official.
newsitem.headline: Japan c/a surplus could pose problems--US official.

text.p: Rises in Japan's current account surplus have the potential to create an explosive situation with the United States, a U.S official said Wednesday.

In an exclusive interview with Reuters Financial Television, Lawrence Greenwood, economic minister-counsellor at the U.S. embassy in Tokyo, said the United States believes Japan's current account surplus will continue to rise into next year.

"Obviously the current account surplus is expanding after decreasing rather dramatically for the last several years... We believe that it is going to continue throughout this year and into next year," Greenwood said.
He said forecasts were never 100 percent certain but said it would be "a matter of concern" if there did turn out to be a reversal in the surplus's recent downward trend.
He said this was an important issue in terms of U.S. and Japanese trade policy and that if the situation got worse it had the potential to explode.

"If the numbers get worse, and we fear they may, that creates an environment in which trade and market access problems...can become serious irritants between our two countries and trade problems are more likely to explode," he said.
"It's like a forest where you haven't had rain for a long time...it only takes a small spark to start a fire and I think that is the kind of environment we seem to be getting into," he added.
Both governments have to work more diligently to solve trade and market access issues quickly before it does become a fire, he said.
Greenwood said that the autumn was a key period to watch movements in the trend of the surplus.
"Then we will get a clear idea of just what the impact, for example, of the rise in the consumption tax will be on domestic demand and just how strong domestic demand is going to be," he said.
Asked whether he agreed with statements by Japanese policy-makers that economic structural reforms were working to bring down the surplus, Greenwood said only time would tell.
"I think the proof is in the pudding and we'll just have to see how it works out," he said.

"Obviously there have been some structural changes in the Japanese economy but whether they are sufficient to really address the structural problems that underly what appears to be a recurring current account surplus is still open to question," he added.
Greenwood said deregulation in Japan was important to reduce trade tensions, adding that although it would not have an immediate impact on macroeconomic numbers, it would improve market access.
Speaking about ongoing talks on telecommunications, medical services and financial services, he also said he was optimistic that there was going to be progress in the short term.
He said the two countries had a mutual interest in Japanese deregulation and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto had expressed his commitment to opening Japan's markets.
